newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - South African strike sends platinum soaring. [CORRECTED 15:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - South African strike sends platinum soaring. [CORRECTED 15:05 GMT]

text.p: A wildcat strike by 4,600 workers at South Africa's Rustenburg Platinum Holdings Ltd, the world's biggest producer, sent platinum prices soaring on Wednesday.
The company said there was no immediate end in sight to the illegal stoppage which started on Monday night, affecting between 15 and 20 percent of production.
"I don't see any solution yet," said Johan Adler, spokesman for holding company Anglo American Platinum Corp Ltd, as workers failed to turn up for their day shifts.

Mining analysts said there was a danger of a protracted shutdown of part at the giant mine 120 km (75 miles) northwest of Johannesburg which has had a troubled history of labour unrest, including a violent three-week strike last July.
"The worst-case scenario is that we have another prolonged strike similar to the one we had last year," said Paul Brogan of BOE NatWest.
"The best-case scenario would be that they go back by the weekend."
News of the strike by workers from two of three hostels on the Amandelbult section of the mine propelled an already tight platinum market through the $400 an ounce level on Wednesday.
Platinum was fixed at $404.50 in London, its highest since August 1, 1996, and up from $398.00 previously.
Palladium, produced alongside platinum, was fixed at its highest level since the official fixings began in 1989 of $188.00, up from $177.50 on Tuesday.
Nickel, which is produced as a by-product in platinum mines, also gained ground on the news of the Rustenburg stoppage.
"There is a great fear of short-term shortages and certainly a strike might heighten those anxieties," said Ross Gardiner, mining analyst at stockbroker SocGen Frankel Pollak.

Precious metal dealers said the strike news had fuelled a scramble to buy or borrow both platinum and palladium, already scarce because of the failure of Russia to export this year due to administrative problems.
Russia is the world's largest palladium exporter and second biggest platinum supplier after South Africa.
Rustenburg produced 690,000 ounces of platinum in the six months to December 31, 1996, equivalent to around a quarter of world supply.
In the financial year to June 30, 1996 Rustenburg produced 698,000 oz of palladium, 149,700 oz of rhodium and 14,100 tonnes of nickel. Platinum production in the same period was 1.553 million oz.
(Corrects figure for nickel from 14.1 tonnes).

The problems at Rustenburg follow the suspension of members of the Mouthpiece Workers' Union and a company manager after an alleged attack on a member of the rival National Union of Mineworkers (NUM).
As a result, the workers did not turn up for Monday's night shift and a fight broke out at one of the hostels between strikers and employees who wanted to work, resulting in several injuries.
Adler said that the NUM was opposed to the strike and he said talks were continuing to try to resolve the issue.
Last year's three-week strike at Rustenburg, with a total workforce of some 28,000, led to the loss of 100,000 ounces of platinum production.
SocGen's Gardiner said the latest unrest was part of a long-term dispute over union representation.

"It's a fight for power between union representatives and non-union representatives. They (mine management) are not going to solve the problem in three weeks. The workers may return in a few days but this is going to be a long process," he said.
Platinum and palladium are used in electronics and autocatalysts for cleaning up car exhaust gases. Platinum is also used for jewellery and palladium for dental alloys.
